author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@VanderHead @mattyglesias I don't know if the people you work with are a representative sample, but regardless, it seems to me you have an issue with university education rather than K-12 education. 

In any case, I don't think the US teaches K-12 students much more math than other countries.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @VanderHead @mattyglesias You might have not used calculus in decades, but you certainly couldn't get your degree in math and physics without it.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@VanderHead @mattyglesias What the US teaches is not so advanced, and certainly Algebra II, pre-calculus, and calculus are meaningful prep for any quantitative major in college. 

These majors are far more popular now than they've ever been, so these topics are more important today than in the past.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mattyglesias So yes you do need a special talent to be Einstein, just like you need a special talent to be a world champion athlete or a great author. But you do not need any special talent to complete the K-12 math curriculum.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mattyglesias I think running is a good analogy. Yes, some people are naturally better at it, but almost everyone is very far from exhausting their potential, and people understand that if they worked harder they could run so much more than they do.

author: boazbaraktcs
boazbaraktcs
text: @mattyglesias Unfortunately, it seems that the main property of "data science" that the CA math changes wants to use is that it is not very well defined, and so you can water down the material as much as you want until you get good test results.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mattyglesias One issue with California is that they try to use "data science" as a way to solve educational gaps. It's a good idea to teach students proficiency with data, but it is not a magic bullet to make students better at the fundamentals of algebra and formal reasoning.

text: @mdsteele47 @adrian_mims @dbressoud The data science pathway will be a form of tracking. And I think a worse one at that, because it's not honest about what it's covering.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@mdsteele47 @adrian_mims @dbressoud Here is where we disagree. Algebra & Calculus are not "outdated", and they are more relevant than ever in the 21st century. Indeed, interest in STEM majors is at an all-time high and rapidly growing.

If you are cutting this material from students, you're doing them a disservice

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mdsteele47 @adrian_mims @dbressoud Also there is a difference between "not all students should take calculus" and "let's structure the system so it's all but impossible for students to take calculus unless they take private out-of-school courses"

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mdsteele47 @adrian_mims @dbressoud This does not justify it at all. There are many issues with the CMF (see https://t.co/3J94uZCpdn ) , but the main thing is that it will funnel students into a "data science" path which may not even provide all of the Algbera II content.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @mdsteele47 @adrian_mims @dbressoud However, there are also many students that take calculus despite not being ready for it. And as @dbressoud  says, it's unclear if they benefit from it. If such students skipped a course to get to calculus, then it was probably detrimental.

text: @shravas @mathillustrated And this is not the only issue. The "data science pathway" is likely to be rejected by affluent districts or students that want to reach calculus. So it will end up being effectively a lower track, that once you chose it in 9th grade, you are locked into.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @shravas @mathillustrated I actually don't think so, but even if you won't take calculus in 12th grade, do you really want to close off that option for students in the 8th grade whose parents don't have the resources to enroll them in a private course?

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @shravas @inhaleopenair @cheesemonkeysf They admit this new 8th grade background will not enough to go into Geometry in 9th grade, but somehow claim that this background would be useful in the 11th grade to compress pre-calculus with Algebra II, or to skip pre-calculus altogether.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @shravas @inhaleopenair @cheesemonkeysf It's a bit of "squaring the circle". If you really taught *all* of the material in Algebra I in 8th grade, then students would simply be ready to take the next course in the sequence in the 9th grade, but they are not claiming they can.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @shravas Yes they say this, but they don't explain how they are going to cover the material and this cannot work. This approach was tried in San Francisco and as @inhaleopenair @cheesemonkeysf can tell you, it didn't work. Calculus AP enrollment fell 13% https://t.co/5WlZjGEEdj

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@shravas @mathillustrated Will try to write more comprehensive answer later.  The document is written in confusing way but if you track actual material, it's not the case.

As a sanity check, if they were truly doing "acceleration for all" then everyone should have had a path to calculus.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@shravas The caveat here is that it's "content" but not "the content". If it was truly the case that they taught Algebra I, then why couldn't students then take Geometry in 9th grade and be able to take calculus?
The answer is that it isn't.

author: boazbaraktcs

text: 4/4 Bottom line is not that quantum computers don't offer computational advantage, but (as many agree) improving fidelity much more important than increasing number of qubits. Also, need other benchmarks than XEB, ideally for tasks that are independently useful!

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 3/4 Also, depending on architecture the classical algorithm may scale *better* than a noisy quantum circuit, meaning that increasing the number of qubits makes the classical XEB better than the noisy quantum one. https://t.co/ktS51ReSSX

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 2/4 we use much less classical resources (single GPU) and still get "in the ballpark" (~ one order of magnitude worse) of cross-entropy benchmark (XEB) results. As in our prior work https://t.co/ci5ftCuJed we spoof the benchmark *without* fully simulating circuit. https://t.co/Gpj4MelgrT

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 12/14 STEM has become more mathematically sophisticated. You now see a gradient in every other CS talk, not to mention bra's, ket's, or elliptic curves. No one knows what math we'll need in future, but the best way to prepare students is to give broad & deep math foundation.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 11/14 There is nothing special about "data science" that makes it more equitable. In fact, it is well known that it can replicate and amplify the biases that already exist in society. Data fluency is good, but making it is a solution to equity is magical thinking.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 10/14 The CMF states that "the data science field provides opportunities for equitable practice, with multiple opportunities for students to pursue answers to wonderings and to accept the reality that all students can excel in data science fields."

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
9/14 The CMF itself describes skills in a high school data science class as "learn to clean data sets" "download and upload data" and develop something they call "data moves".

These vocational skills are no replacement to basic mathematical ways of thinking.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
8/14 Am not against data science, but courses promoted by CA don't build lasting foundations, but rather teach to eyeball data and use spreadsheets & other tools that will likely be obsolete by the time students finish college.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 7/14 I am also not a "calculus fanatic" - I think probability,  discrete math, logic, can all be great ways to get math maturity needed for college STEM. But these topics are conceptually as hard or more as calculus. They do not require less math skills or preparation.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@rrwilliams Neither me nor anyone really can or should set a universal policy. Many conferences already use openreview and I’m advocating for more of them to do so and/or require arxiving of submissions. 

But there will always be many venues with varying policies to fit particular cases

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 4/4 This bottleneck shouldn't stop or slow science. Papers can still be made public, read, used, and cited. This is what arXiv is great at. Let arXiv handle dissemination, and let conferences or other mechanisms help with the limited resource of attention.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 3/4 Conferences and peer review do a decent job at filtering & highlighting papers to relevant communities. (At least less bad than any other way I know of.)  But they necessarily create a bottleneck: peer review takes time, and for filtering to be useful, most papers rejected

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 2/4 Scarce resources are a fact of life we need to deal with, but no need for un-necessary scarcity. Attention is scarce, bits on the Internet for PDFs are not.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @jfitzsimons We know of course that if NP=P then we can break cryptography. The question is how would you demonstrate a function F in NP∩coNP (or AM∩coAM) such that you can break the encryption using F as an oracle. This should be a uniform function, not parameterized by public key.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
20/20 Bottom line is that right now we do have candidates for post-quantum secure public-key encryption. But this could all change with a single algorithm, and we can't "rest easy" 

As I say in my survey, better understanding of PKE is urgent&important! 

https://t.co/8RbUorcvei

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
19/20 For more on relations of PKE and proof systems (SZK++) see the fascinating work of Berman et al 

https://t.co/51TZRCBUl9 https://t.co/mkzIC04LdJ

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
18/20 For such systems, distinguishing between fake&real public keys can be reduced to statistical distance and so they can be broken in  SZK ⊆ AM∩coAM.

However, other systems (including my own and McEliece) are not known to be broken in AM∩coAM.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 17/20 In a public key system, if E0 and E1 are the distributions of encryptions of 0&1 respectively, they will be far. However in many lattice based systems one can generate a "fake public key" under which they are essentially identical (and decryption is impossible)

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 16/20 This is because the "statistical distance" problem is in SZK. This is the task of, given two randomized circuits E0&E1, of distinguishing between the case they induce statistically near and far distributions.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 15/20 However, this assumes that we can recognize valid key/ciphertext pairs (e,c). This is the case for RSA but not necessarily for lattice based schemes. Still many lattice-based schemes can also be broken in NP∩coNP (or its cousin SZK ⊆ AM∩coAM).

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 14/20 As Goldreich-Goldwasser https://t.co/eEdvAKgsRu say, there is an old intuition from Brassard for (b) along following lines: if e is public-key and c is ciphertext, can certify that c is NOT an encryption of 1, by showing that it's an encryption of 0.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 13/20 We have no evidence for (a), but let me also say why we don't know (b) either. ("We have no evidence" is not the same as "we have evidence that not"!)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
12/20 However people are understandably worried whether there is something inherently incompatible between quantum computation and public-key encryption. In particular some in that thread suggested that maybe:
(a) NP∩coNP ⊆ BQP
(b) All PKEs can be broken in NP∩coNP

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
11/20 However:
1) Shor's algorithm doesn't affect private-key crypto.
2) We can construct public-key signatures based on private-key objects such as one-way functions or hash functions (though with cost in efficiency https://t.co/OJx86mvIyn). 
3) We still have lattices/coding!

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 10/20 Famously @PeterShor1 showed that quantum computers can break two out of the three main families of public-key encryption: factoring , discrete log, and lattice/coding.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 9/20 People have looked at constructing other public-key encryptions, and I myself have proposed one (see https://t.co/tqoLY5s89P with Applebaum & Wigderson). But how secure these are and/or how different they are from others is still open question.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 8/20 Essentially most constructions can be thought of as variants of either Diffie-Hellman, RSA, or Robert McEliece's system from 1978. The latter one is based on error correcting codes, and is related to other lattice/coding based systems. https://t.co/J4b7vny01l

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
7/20 The fact that these two independent lines stumbled across same constructions can be surprising, but in fact even 50 years later, we don't have that many more candidates for public key encryption schemes. 

https://t.co/8RbUorcvei https://t.co/1Fx0whLb8U

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 6/20 In late 1960's, James Ellis of British CESG had very similar thoughts https://t.co/vXbGRO01OZ. He realized PKE is not impossible, but didn't have a construction. First construction was by Cliford Cocks who "pre-discovered" RSA. Later Malcolm Williams pre-discovered D&H. https://t.co/u2Wm2JQDu5

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 5/20 Merkle, and Diffie&Hellman realized that PKE is not fundamentally impossible, but didn't know how it would be possible. Luckily, D&H got a great tip from their colleague John Gill to use modular exponentiation, which led to Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange https://t.co/grMCGIE3sh

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 4/20 When Berkeley undergraduate Ralph Merkle proposed it as a course project in 1974, it was rejected out of hand. When he submitted it to the CACM, the reviewer comments were that  “Experience shows that it is extremely dangerous to transmit key information in the clear.”

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 3/20 Public-key encryption is another beast altogether. First, its hard to overstate how revolutionary it was. Unlike heavier-than-air flight or many other inventions, despite cryptography's thousands year old history, PKE was not even *imagined*

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 2/20 Private key encryption often boils down to simply combining many non-local and non-linear operations. Making it efficient is challenging but if willing to lose some, a Monkey with a typewriter could probably construct a block cipher. See  https://t.co/rEW60HLVEl by @wtgowers

There is a fundamental gulf between public and private key encryption. https://t.co/ygixcwW3vq

quoted.text: @mattyhoban @dabacon @rdviii I think you’re missing the big picture here. In public key crypto you encrypt using some known function of the public key and the plaintext. author: boazbaraktcs
text: @jfitzsimons @LittleDetritus @dabacon @rdviii @BenCriger @hyperelliptic @hashbreaker I think it would change power structure of the web. A typical user would only exchange public keys with few large companies (Apple, Google, Microsoft etc) and all communication would go through them.

text:

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@jfitzsimons @LittleDetritus @dabacon @rdviii @BenCriger @hyperelliptic @hashbreaker Digital signatures can be built from one-way functions (and more efficiently from hash funcs), so there's no reason to think that quantum will break them

text: 15/21 Traditional "optimizing compilers" are bounded by (1) optimized code must be semantically equivalent and (2) most code is not perf bottleneck anyway. In contrast in ML (1) everything is approximate anyway and (2) training is hugely expensive.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 14/21 Jonathan Frankle (https://t.co/8XqGbDIfVW @jefrankle) surprised the world of ML with his and advisor Carbin's "lottery ticket" paper. But his works extends far beyond. It exploits the fact that ML deals with *approximate computation* to get radically superior optimization

author: boazbaraktcs

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 9/21 In particular Anurag made great advances on "area laws" which show that for "natural" quantum states (arising from low dim geometries), the entanglement between two parts is bounded by their boundary. https://t.co/TSUNTUBLq7

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 8/21 Quantum mechanics are the foundations of our universe, and yet at large scale it always looks classical. Anurag Anshu (https://t.co/CNzn4Eq8nV , @AnuragAnshu4) works on understanding this puzzle, combining quantum many-body systems with constraint-satisfaction problems. https://t.co/0vj4KPDTVo

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 6/21 Optimal transport is about mapping distribution X' to X while minimizing some distance. In particular OT allows using an algorithm designed for X on data coming from X'. This comes in handy if e.g. X is well-resourced language but X' is one with sparser data https://t.co/dh8Op9xCr1

author: boazbaraktcs

text: @soashworth @beenwrekt First take on average-case analysis is often default clean distribution, such as random graphs, but then often people try to look at parameterized distribution (e.g., the probability of an edge), and then go to more sophisticated versions as well (eg stochastic block model).

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
4/ 4

To me, whether we view the generative models as corresponding to beliefs or to some approximation of how input was actually generated, is a second order consideration.

Once you are willing to assign probabilities in retrospect, you're not a frequentist anymore.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3/4

Bayesians are more "liberal" and are willing to accept "backward looking probabilities", where one is given a data and we retro-fit the generative model to the data.

This is the view behind average-case analysis of heuristics such as SAT solvers.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
2/4 In such algorithm, we think of input as worst-case, and only randomness is over coins of algorithm which is completely under our control. 

This is in contrast to average-case analysis of algorithms (that can be randomized or deterministic)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
1/4 Maybe answer deserves 🧵. My view is "frequentist" analysis holds probabilities to the highest standards. 

You can only talk about "forward-looking probabilities" in the sense that they are defined by first "pre-registering" an experiment, such as a randomized algorithm.

quoted.text: @boazbaraktcs Let me turn the question around: if you were to analyze the running time of a randomized algorithm, would that make you a Bayesian or a Frequentist?

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@beenwrekt Analyzing randomized algorithms on worst-case input is Frequentist- only randomness you analyze is coin tosses of the algorithm, which is a distribution perfectly under your control.

Average-case analysis is often (not always) Bayesian, since input dist is often on beliefs

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @beenwrekt To what extent is "algorithmic perspective" (population is fixed, we control the randomness) the same as frequentism, and "generative model perspective" (randomness over knowledge/beliefs) same as Bayesanism?

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 12/12 Finally the 10 year award goes to Aaronson and Arkhipov's STOC 11 paper on Boson Sampling. Once again this is about the permanent. They show that the computational difficulty of sampling the permanent can be used to give evidence for quantum speedups! https://t.co/Vbnx28LsXV

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 11/12 Thorup and Zwick's paper studies the question of computing distances in large graph. Sure we can solve all pairs shortest paths, but that would require quadratic time. They showed a near-linear pre-processing that enables answering any distance query.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 10/12 The first poly-time algorithm was Khachiyan's ellipsoid algorithm in 1979. It was & is much worse than simplex in practice, but it gave rise to interior point methods which can now often beat simplex on practical instances.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
9/12 S&T gave a partial explanation by showing Simplex runs in poly-time if the inputs are perturbed, thereby initiating the field of smoothed analysis. 

Interestingly, for a long time it was not known if there is a poly-time algorithm for linear programming.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 8/12 Spielman and Teng's work deals with one of best algorithmic stories of all times. The Simplex algorithm for linear programming was invented by Danzing in WW II. It's everyone's favorite example of an algorithm that is exponential in the worst case but efficient in practice. https://t.co/tKdQyQVHVo

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
7/12 Permanent is defined by a formula very similar to determinant except the absence of some -1 factors (see https://t.co/KGPPNvd1mg ) but unlike determinant, it's very hard to compute & even approximate. 

Paper shows difficulty almost disappears if matrix is non negative https://t.co/DDu4WOYl0s

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
6/12 20 year award goes to STOC 2001 papers of Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda, Spielman-Teng, and Thorup-Zwick.

Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda deals with one of TCS's favorite problems - the matrix permanent. It's a great example of the power and peril of negative numbers.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
5/12 The STOC 88 & 89 papers above showed that we can obtain information-theoretically secure secure multiparty computation (MPC) if large enough fraction is honest. 

See @LindellYehuda's survey for more https://t.co/nJTJWVKSD5

author: boazbaraktcs

4/12 What does this mean? That any collection of parties that do not trust each other, can still perform an arbitrary joint computation on their private inputs. 

This was established under assumptions by Yao & Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson. Surprisingly sometimes can do without!

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3/12 These papers were part of the "crypto revolution" of the 1980s, when crypto extended beyond encryption & signatures to general protocol problems.

Arguably the fundamental theorem of cryptography is that we can simulate a virtual trusted third party.

text: 7/7 ** By "stitching together" we (following Lenc-Vedaldi) mean combining two parts using a trainable layer. But this is not full "fine tuning" since the layer is simple (low capacity) and so cannot by itself be used to fit the data. See paper for more details. https://t.co/iw1n0SyvPN

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 6/7 *Stitching not only approach to study this question - can use measures such as CKA https://t.co/m0SzBbinq2 but stitching has some advantages. Can identify similarity even in cases where representations are "far" by CKA, and also say when one rep is "better" than another. https://t.co/e2Limspu29

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
5/7 We call (B) "More is better". We show that when replacing bottom layers of net N with layers from N' that was trained using different data, epochs, or width, then performance changes accordingly. 

In particular if N' has sufficiently "more" of resource, then perf improves! https://t.co/GuDJrxUWJu

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
4/7 We call (A) "All roads lead to Rome". 

For example, we can "stitch together"** bottom k layers of depth-d network trained with self-supervised methods with the top (d-k) layers of supervised-trained network with same architecture. Get minor accuracy drop for all k. https://t.co/iN9EKj70cR

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3/7 Several works (eg @ch402's) point to 2nd scenario, but hard to quantify*
We test two predictions:

(A) Representations learned through different means (e.g. self-supervised vs supervised) should be compatible
(B) Representations learned with more data/compute should be better

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
7/7 Note: Modeling NISQ as quantum local algorithms is mathematically clean but abstracts away:
1) Some platforms (e.g. Lukin's) have non-local constraints
2) This model assumes noise is constant and size → ∞ but current NISQ have small size
3) Computation graph ≠ instance

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
6/7 Paper raises many open questions, but for me the most important one is this one (for both max-cut and other CSPs). 

We believe there exists a "NISQ sampling advantage" but is there a "NISQ optimization advantage"? https://t.co/pIoQAauogJ

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
5/7 Also show ∃ classical alg (implicit in  Aizenman, Lebowitz, and Ruelle 1987 and Lyons 2017) achieving 2/π≈0.63.  

While 0.63 < 0.71, interestingly in experiments, ALR algorithm often matches or beats QAOA even for locality>1 and graphs with small girth. https://t.co/aFrdKWzA9b

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
4/7 We show a limitation of 1-local quantum algorithms and an improved classical algorithm.

For D-regular high-girth graphs, any local alg outputs cut of value 1/2 + C/√D.   C can be at most Parisi constant ≈ 0.76. We show no 1-local quantum alg can achieve > 0.71. https://t.co/0sgcypxHd3

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3/7 For given optimization problem, question is whether exists *any instance* where a quantum local alg such as QAOA beats all classical algs

In the paper we focus on max cut on high-girth regular graphs, and make small steps on this question. https://t.co/3e0gtOZwCQ

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
2/7 We model NISQ devices as local quantum algorithms - qubits are associated with graph, and every output depends only on vertices of distance at most some radius r. 

(See note at end of thread and discussion in Sec 1.3 of paper.)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
1/7 We believe simulating the probability distribution induced by NISQ devices is classically hard. 

In recent paper with @kmarwahaha we ask whether it's hard to match their optimization performance.

https://t.co/FWlNOMACF8

(Spoiler: We don't answer it but see 🧵)

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Demographic and opinion changes in Israel mean that there is no longer a realistic chance for a left-wing government. The best we can hope for is probably a  center-right-left coalition of the type that we're getting now. I hope it works.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Nitzan Horvitz - leader of Meretz - the party I used to vote for when I lived in Israel. I remember those times when the left still had a fighting chance and in every election we did not know which side will win.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Merav Michaeli- the labor party was the dominant party in Israel from its founding until 1977 and a major party until Ehud Barak (another disappointing general) nearly led to its extinction. At least it survived even if its leader will have to be minister of transportation

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Benny Gantz - one of many generals in Israel's history who became disappointing politicians - he betrayed his coalition partners and voters in joining Netanyahu last time, but gets to keep his defense ministry

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Mansour Abbas - head of United Arab Party, a political party of the (more moderate southern branch of) Islamic Movement - offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood (Hamas is another offshoot). However, they decided to focus on bettering the status of Israel's  Arab population.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Bennet, Lieberman & Saar - They worked closely with Netnayahu and B&L are more right-wing than him. Lieberman's slogan used to be "no loyalty - no citizenship" which is as bad as it sounds. But they all hate Netanyahu enough to sit with..

author: boazbaraktcs
text: Yair Lapid - I've always thought he had a huge ego but despite getting 17 seats, he sacrificed the PM position to Bennet that has only 7 seats (actually maybe 6 given defections) to achieve the goal of unseating Netanyahu

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
The apparently formed new Israeli coalition is one of the strangest combination of bedfellows, united only by their hatred of Netanyahu. But who knows, maybe that what's it takes for the country to heal.

For non-Israelis, these are the signatories: 🧵 https://t.co/ETfAuY5lsR

quoted.text: And this is it folks: Lapid told the President he has succeeded in forming a new government - for the first time in 12 years WITHOUT NETANYAHU. Though there's still more than a week to iron all details (or mess up)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@algo_class @jasondhartline Conceptually I agree with @algo_class that if you have only one lecture, you can describe reductions as building algorithm for G using function calls to F.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@yoavgo @TaliaRinger It is bland but not harmful. It’s a situation where “perfect is enemy of the good”. 

The goal is not that authors write a whole separate paper on ethics. It is that they take the time to consider positive and negative potential ethical implications  of their work.

text: 10/12 To give an analogy, while I personally oppose the BDS movement, I respect people that support it. They are free to sign petitions and to personally refuse to travel to Israel or to work on joint projects with Israeli institutions.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 9/12 I think that unless a person that behaves in this way recognizes the harm and apologizes for it, they should not get a personal award (as opposed to an award given to a paper or book), and especially the highest award in the field.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 8/12 He also explicitly called for blocking admission of Iranian students, claiming that "Iranians who did not leave Iran when the religious fanatics took over ... may well be sympathetic to Iran’s desires to build a nuclear weapon and ... for terrorists" (see letter)

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 7/12 As the letter details, for many years he was well known by the Iranian community for his offensive responses to potential students.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
6/12 This is enabled since by and large, scientists are able to treat students and colleagues as individuals, independently of their background and country of origins.

It is unfortunately clear now that Jeff Ullman was not able to maintain that distinction.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 5/12 Through my time in this field, I was exposed to beautiful ideas and got to work with amazing collaborators. I've written papers with people from many backgrounds, including orthodox Jews, Iranian Muslims, and even VI users 😃

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 4/12 The Turing award is not just about technical achievements, but is about celebrating a person. Turing laurates are widely honored, and considered the representatives of our field to both outsiders and new students.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 3/12 In fact, the letter I signed does not even take a position if the award should be withdrawn or not. I am unsure what I think though believe it should not have been given in the first place.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
2/12 One of my first exposures to theoretical computer science was through the Hopcroft-Ullman book, and I remain grateful to Ullman for it.

I appreciate Ullman's contributions to the field, and do not want to "cancel" him.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @roydanroy @whybansal I like this question also because it promotes a "separation of concerns". Over-parameterization happens at the level of representation learning (= pretraining), while it might not be a necessary feature for adapting to a specific task.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @roydanroy @whybansal It is quite interesting to understand whether in such cases there is another notion of "simplicity" that would still capture both good performance and small gap.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @roydanroy @whybansal BTW I don't think that self-supervision + linear probe are the ultimate solution for very problem. There are many situations where linear probes perform significantly worse than fine tuning.

author: boazbaraktcs
boazbaraktcs
text:
@roydanroy @whybansal To me main points on SSS are:

1) The generalization error is small

2) Test error quite similar to supervised learning (e.g., test in left & right side of gif similar, SSS vs supervised gap 0.7 points in best variant in this table)

3) It's natural- not invented to achieve 1&2 https://t.co/O9truiU1h8

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @kareem_carr For example, if you are a lender, what you “want your model to be doing” might be to maximize expected profits. But given data at hand, this could mean discriminating against populations, in which case the algorithm is “unfair” even if it’s unbiased. See https://t.co/LgdFBtz7kV

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @kareem_carr Yes I think this is a reason why algorithmic fairness researchers try to avoid the term “bias”. It has a statistical meaning that doesn’t correspond to the colloquial meaning in the context of preventing discrimination.

text:
@ajaydiv @mattyglesias I see no evidence that (for example) majoring in humanities yields better individuals than computer science. 

What I think our role as computer science educators is:

2) Model that we care about more than just metrics

@nikitab @bryan_caplan There are cheaper ways to do it than to get them through 4 years.

author: boazbaraktcs

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @nikitab @bryan_caplan High level point testing Caplan’s theory doesn’t require re-organizing all of society. Even though we can’t time travel to the 1950s, hire high school students and see if they are just as good, there is enough variety in access to education that we can “space travel”.

If an employer could hire people out of high school, they could pay them much less and get many more useful years out of them.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 12/ I think that a society in which students are educated is a better one, and that along the way students get skills, and framework of knowledge  that make it easier for them to acquire new skills. I admit I have no proof for this, but employers & 100-year history seem to agree.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 11/ Here I am biased. I think education is its own good, and it’s an inherent good for a student to see the proof of Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem, or understand the analysis of the multiplicative weights update method.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 10/ To be sure - students actually do learn these topics in college. We do see how sophomores know more than first-years, and juniors more than sophomores. There is a reason courses have prerequisites. But is it “useful” for them to learn these topics?

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 9/ Not just “theory” topics such as Turing machines, halting problem and NP completeness. Whether it’s functional programming, designing recursive algorithms, writing assembler code by hand, or analyzing backpropagation, we routinely teach topics that 90% of developers don’t use.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
8/ Finally, here is where @bryan_caplan is correct. People don’t use most of what they learn in high school & beyond.

Even in a supposedly “useful” major like computer science, I estimate that 90% of the time in their jobs, our graduates use less than 10% of topics we teach.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 7/  If conscientiousness & conformity are traits that are important to an employer, these are traits that *can* be developed. It’s just that the army does a much better job developing them than universities.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
6/ What is it that college signals? Caplan says it’s conscientiousness & conformity.

My wife is physical therapist that used to work a lot with the coast guard. Her patients always came 15 minutes early and were exceedingly polite.  My Harvard students? Not so much.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 5/ Businesses can also take advantage without waiting for different policies. Most people don’t move far from their home. By placing your firm in areas with lower educational opportunities, you can find less educated workers that still have whatever it is that college “signals”

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 4/ There is simple policy prescription to take advantage of this inefficiency - a country that stops formal education at 8th grade & taxes/abolishes college, should get huge productivity boost. “Amazingly” countries with vastly varying cultures & regimes all doing the opposite.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 3/ Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and this claim is indeed extraordinary. If Caplan is right then societies around the world are wasting 10-20% of people’s working years and hundreds of Billions of dollars for this useless signaling game.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: 2/ Caplan’s theory that about 80% of education beyond basic literacy and numeracy is just about “useless signaling”. It serves no useful purpose by itself. Rather students and employers get stuck in “arms race” of requiring ever more credentials to do jobs that don’t need them.

@scottlegrand @thomasahle @zzznah No because you contract along the a axis. This generalizes the fact that when you multiply n × k matrix A and a k × m matrix B then you contract along the k-length ax and get an n × m matrix. 

Nice thing is this automatically handles “extra axes” such as batches, attention heads

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@thomasahle @zzznah If A and B are tensors that share axis a, A⊙ₐ B denotes the tensor  obtained by contracting them along a axis.

If A and B are vectors with a as their only ax, A⊙ₐ B is their dot product. If A has {a,b} and B has {a,c} then A⊙ₐ B is their matrix product with axes {b,c}

text:
12/12

They show that for several popular hierarchical clustering algorithms, they can get bounds on the interval that translate to good bounds on p. In single-cell data, when there is no signal, their p value high even if standard tiny. When there is, p values are comparable. https://t.co/g16Sb5bwqB

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
11/12

If the algorithm is stable, then there is an interval corresponding to α ∈ [a,b] in which the algorithm still outputs A. Conditioning on X in this interval makes calculating  P[ ‖μ(A)‖ ≥ θ ] easy. T

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
10/12

To get a sense, let's  consider baby case that data is X~N(0,I) and instead of clustering, algorithm outputs single set A and we want to bound P[ ‖μ(A)‖ ≥ θ | A].
Suppose μ(A)=v. We consider the one-dimensional affine subspace S = { X + αv⋅1_A for α∈ℝ }.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
9/12

Reminiscent of differential-privacy based guarantees for safe hypothesis generation (@Aaroth & @mrtz can weigh in) but they consider deterministic clustering. Also also don't want to create new alg but analyze algs biologists already use & even give code (or at least R 😃)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
8/12 

They consider clustering algorithms that take collection X of vectors and have some stability properties, in the sense that if you shift some subset of vectors by a small vector v, you will still get the same clustering.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
7/12

This is what they want to do, and under assumptions, they manage to bound  P[ ‖ μ(A)−μ(B)‖ ≥ θ | clustering produces A,B  and more ] where "more" is additional conditions to make computation tractable.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
6/12

Problem is that your clustering algorithm depends on the numbers, and conditioned on getting A and B, the p value that μ(A)-μ(B)>1.6 is actually large.
Arguably right thing is to compute P[ ‖ μ(A)−μ(B)‖ ≥ θ | clustering produces A,B ] .

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
5/12
But standard methods will tell you that with tiny p value, the two clusters really are different & you can (wrongly) rule out the null hypothesis that data is random numbers.

Happens also with single cell & even Penguins 😃 https://t.co/O5dhj3HPw7

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
4/12
Here is a simple example why things could go wrong. Imagine data is just 100 numbers from N(0,1),
and we partition it to two clusters A and B - the positive and negative numbers. Unsurprisingly, the mean of A will be about 1.6 larger than B's mean.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3/12 
For example, in single-cell sequencing (which I first learned of from @mor_nitzan), we get a collection of gene-expression vectors for all cells in a tissue.
We cluster these vectors and then hope the clustering corresponds to cells with different functions.

Classical statistics textbook approach is to sit in your armchair, come up with hypothesis, and then test it.

Counter take - the success of deep learning and SAT solvers is evidence for P≠NP and that maybe we actually understand algorithms better than we think

author: boazbaraktcs
text: For both deep learning and SAT, most of time they succeed in tasks that humans can already do, but maybe on bigger scale. Deep learning usually used for human-doable tasks. SAT solvers often also prove theorems such as correctness of programs that humans could in principle do.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: The possibility of P=NP is because there could be a "surprising" algorithm. If we knew that GD and friends were optimal, then there are no surprises, and we would actually be much closer to a "complete" theory of what's computationally feasible and not.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
Your goal as author is to ensure:

1) Beginning of paper clarifies what you did and why it’s important

2) Remainder shows reviewer you dotted your i’s and crossed your t’s and so they can trust you to have done thorough work in experiments, theory, and literature search.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: I believe that often (not always!) by page 2 or so, the reviewer already knows if they want to accept or reject, and at this point are looking for more evidence to confirm this belief.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
3) Know reader’s context - the only thing you can assume your reviewer knows is other papers in the same conference, so paper should be written to look like these papers. Reviewer has expectation to find things in Figure 1 etc

(Still struggling w this personally for ML papers)

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
1) “Front load” contributions - reader should get gist as early as possible. Should know result from abstract and why they should care by page 2.

2) No surprises - paper is not mystery novel - shouldn’t spring up important contributions, caveats or relevant prior work late.

author: boazbaraktcs

If a field is growing exponentially, there will necessarily be many more submissions than qualified people to review them.

So, reviewing will suck no matter what we do.

@yoavgo @chrmanning @roydanroy @mraginsky @ylecun @SeeTedTalk @ChrisGPotts @aclmeeting 4. A conference doesn't exist in a vacuum. Prohibiting arxiv submissions drives out researchers from other communities where arxiv is part of norms.

5. DB is not only tool to combat reviewing bias. More transparency (e.g. openreview) also helps in review quality & consistency.

author: boazbaraktcs
text: @yoavgo @chrmanning @roydanroy @mraginsky @ylecun @SeeTedTalk @ChrisGPotts @aclmeeting 3. Double-blind reviewing is also not a "magic bullet", and is inherently imperfect. That's OK.  It  only becomes a problem if in pursuit of (anyway unattainable) perfection one hinders open science & brings us back to the days of emailing papers to your friends.

author: boazbaraktcs
boazbaraktcs
text:
@thesasho @roydanroy @ylecun @yoavgo @SeeTedTalk @chrmanning @ChrisGPotts @aclmeeting Yes these issues existed before arxiv, except worse since not everyone had access to the process.

Things were even worse before email. One example: places like MIT had effectively later conference deadlines, since they coordinated a courier to deliver paper submissions to the PC

author: boazbaraktcs
boazbaraktcs
text:
@yoavgo @SeeTedTalk @chrmanning @ChrisGPotts @aclmeeting Moreover, overall arxiv has democratizing effect on science, helping balance power. It gives access to people less connected, and ability to make their contribution and avoid being scooped.

In “good old days” connected people or PC members had access to manuscripts months ahead.

author: boazbaraktcs
text:
@yoavgo @SeeTedTalk @chrmanning @ChrisGPotts @aclmeeting Some theory conferences don’t do double-blind, some do (CRYPTO has for ages), but they all allow & encourage arxiv posting. 

Arxiv complicated double blind, but doesn’t make it impossible, just like the possibility of sometimes guessing author names doesn’t.
